title: Columns that add nothing
prompt:
Before fitting a model, find the feature columns that add no information: those that are linear combinations of the columns before them. Fitting with one of them in the matrix makes the coefficients non-unique.

Write `redundant_columns(X, names, rtol=1e-8)`. `X` has shape (n, p) and `names` holds its p column names. Walk through the columns from left to right, and return the names of the columns that don't increase the rank of the columns kept so far. An all-zero column is redundant.

Columns come in wildly different units (an energy counter in watt-hours next to a valve fraction), so scale every column to unit length before testing. Use `np.linalg.matrix_rank` with its `rtol=` argument, which sets the tolerance relative to the largest singular value.
hints: Keep a list of the columns that have earned their place. A new column earns it only if adding it makes the kept set's rank go up by one.

Rank in floating point needs a tolerance: singular values below rtol × (largest singular value) count as zero. That comparison is unfair when one column is 10¹⁰ times bigger than another, so divide each column by its norm first. Check for zero-norm columns before dividing.

norms = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=0). Loop j over the columns: skip (as redundant) if norms[j] == 0; otherwise cand = kept + [j]; Z = X[:, cand] / norms[cand]; keep j if np.linalg.matrix_rank(Z, rtol=rtol) == len(cand), else it's redundant.

misconceptions.dummy-variable-trap: An intercept plus one indicator column per category is rank deficient: the indicators always sum to the intercept column. Drop one category, or drop the intercept.
misconceptions.rank-needs-scaling: Numerical rank compares singular values with a tolerance relative to the largest one. Columns on scales 10¹⁰ apart make the small one look like rounding noise; scale columns first.
